persona_data.Name: Maria Santos
persona_data.Problem: Maria feels invisible in her own home after her adult children moved back during the pandemic and never left, eroding her sense of autonomy and personal space.
persona_data.Person Details: Maria is a 58-year-old retired school aide in Sacramento, CA. Her two adult children (ages 29 and 32) returned home in 2020 and remain. She no longer cooks what she wants, watches TV in her room to avoid conflict, and has stopped inviting friends over. She describes herself as 'a guest in my own house.' Her husband sides with the children. She hasn't articulated this as a problem to any professional.
persona_data.Ethnographic Solution: Conduct a spatial ethnography of the home: map how Maria moves through physical space over one week using time-geography diaries and floor plan annotations. Use photo-elicitation interviews where Maria photographs spaces that feel 'hers' vs. 'taken.' Follow with narrative life history interviews. Co-map the temporal rhythms of the household to identify structural interventions for reclaiming space and schedule.

conversation.question: Hello. I would like to understand your situation better. What is your name?
conversation.answer: My name is Maria Santos. Nice to meet you.

conversation.question: How old are you, and what part of your life feels most affected right now?
conversation.answer:
I'm 58 years young. To be honest, it's hard for me to pinpoint exactly which part of my life feels most affected, but I'd say it's a combination of things. It started when my kids came back home during the pandemic. They're both adults, so I thought they'd just be here temporarily until things got back to normal. But that was over two years ago, and they still haven't left.

It's been really tough on me because I feel like I'm losing myself in this situation. I used to love cooking and trying out new recipes, but now my kids are always asking me what's for dinner, and if it's something they can eat or not. It feels like I'm just a servant in my own home.

I've also stopped doing things I enjoy because of the tension that comes with living with them. Like, I used to love watching TV in my room, but now I have to do it there so I don't disturb them. And if they're watching something loud or rowdy, I'll just go back to my room and watch something else. It's like I'm a guest in my own house, you know?

conversation.question: What problem is bothering you the most at the moment?
conversation.answer:
You know, it's hard to pinpoint one thing that's really bothering me right now. But if I had to choose...I think what's eating away at me the most is feeling like I'm losing my sense of self and autonomy in my own home. It's like I've become invisible, you know? My kids are always here, and they're not leaving anytime soon. And it feels like my husband is taking their side more and more often.

It's hard to explain, but it's like I used to be the one who made decisions around the house, who cooked meals, who did things for myself. Now, it feels like everything revolves around them, and I'm just along for the ride. It's frustrating because I feel like I'm still the same person I've always been, but somehow, my life has changed so much.

I know it sounds silly, but sometimes I'll be doing something, like cooking dinner or watching TV, and I'll catch myself thinking, "Wait a minute, this is what my kids do." It's like I'm losing touch with who I am and what makes me happy. And that's really hard for me to deal with.

conversation.question: Can you give me one concrete recent example that shows this problem clearly?
conversation.answer:
.. recently, I was trying to make a simple breakfast for myself, just some scrambled eggs and toast. But my daughter came into the kitchen and started telling me what she thought I should be making instead - something with sausage or bacon, because "that's what you used to make when they were kids." And then she proceeded to tell me how to cook it, like I was some kind of novice again.

It really got under my skin, because I know exactly how to make scrambled eggs and toast. But she just wouldn't listen to me, kept telling me that I was doing it wrong. It felt so... infantilizing. And then, when I finally managed to get the eggs cooked just right, she came over and started tasting them and giving me feedback on how I could improve them.

It was like she thought I needed her permission to even make a simple breakfast for myself. It made me feel so small and insignificant in my own home.

agent1.problem_summary: Feeling invisible and losing autonomy in her own home after adult children moved back during the pandemic, eroding her sense of personal space.
agent1.final_problem_statement: Losing touch with who she is and what makes her happy due to constant involvement from her adult children and feeling like a 'guest' in her own house.

family_relationships.question: Can you tell me about a time when your relationship with one of your adult children was particularly strained or difficult, and how you navigated that situation?
family_relationships.answer:
.. (pausing, reflecting on the past) Well, I'd say it's been pretty much every day since they moved back home. But if I had to choose a specific time... (sighing)

I think it was about six months ago when my daughter and I got into an argument over something silly. She wanted me to help her move some boxes in the garage, and I told her I wasn't going to do it because I'd already done enough physical labor for the day. But she just wouldn't take no for an answer, kept asking me and getting more and more upset.

Finally, I lost my patience and told her that if she couldn't respect my boundaries, then maybe she should just do it herself. (shaking head) It was a stupid thing to say, but at the time, I was feeling really frustrated and overwhelmed.

She stormed off, and we didn't speak for hours. But eventually, we talked it out, and I apologized for being short-tempered. She forgave me, of course, because that's what mothers do, right? (laughing slightly)

But the thing is... even though we made up, the argument still felt like a big deal to me. It made me realize how much tension there was between us, and how hard it was for me to set boundaries with my own child. It's like I'm constantly walking on eggshells around her, trying not to hurt her feelings or make her angry.

It's been really tough, because I feel like I should be able to have a normal relationship with my daughter, but instead, I'm always worried about what she'll think or say next. And it's not just that - it's also feeling like I'm losing myself in the process. Like, who am I anymore if I'm just constantly trying to please my kids?

family_relationships.question: Can you tell me more about what you mean by 'losing touch with who she is and what makes her happy'? What are some things that used to bring her joy or fulfillment, but might be harder for her to access now?
family_relationships.answer:
(pauses, reflecting on the question) You know, I think when I was younger, I loved gardening. I would spend hours in my backyard, tending to my flowers and vegetables, watching them grow and flourish. It was so therapeutic for me, and it made me feel connected to nature. But now... (shrugs) I don't have the time or energy to do that anymore. My kids are always asking me to help them with something, whether it's running errands or fixing things around the house, and I just can't seem to find the time for myself.

And cooking used to be a big part of my life too. I loved trying out new recipes and experimenting with different flavors and ingredients. But now... (sighs) My kids are always asking me what's for dinner, and if it's something they can eat or not. It feels like I'm just a servant in my own home, like I don't have any say in what goes on.

I also used to love reading. I would spend hours curled up with a good book, getting lost in another world. But now... (pauses) I don't really have the time or energy for that anymore either. My kids are always asking me to help them with something, and I just can't seem to find the time for myself.

It's funny, because when my kids were younger, they would always be so excited about things like gardening and cooking and reading. But now... (shrugs) They're all grown up, and it seems like those things are just a distant memory for them. And I'm left feeling like I've lost touch with who I am and what makes me happy.

(looks down, her voice barely above a whisper) It's hard to explain, but sometimes I feel like I'm just going through the motions of life, without any real sense of purpose or fulfillment. Like, I'm just existing in my own home, rather than really living there.

emotions.question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt truly happy and fulfilled, before your adult children became involved in your daily life?
emotions.answer:
(pauses, looking up with a soft smile) Oh, that's a wonderful question. You know, I think one of the happiest times for me was when my kids were younger, but still living away from home. They would come visit us on weekends or during school breaks, and it was always such a joy to spend time with them.

I remember one particular summer, my daughter was about 10 years old, and she had just learned how to ride a bike. She was so excited to show off her new skill to me, and we spent hours riding around the neighborhood together, laughing and feeling carefree. It was such a special moment for both of us.

And then there were the holidays. We would always have big family gatherings, with all of our extended family coming over to celebrate. Those were always so much fun, with lots of food, laughter, and just a general sense of warmth and connection.

But I think what really stands out in my mind is when I was still working as a school aide. I loved my job, and it gave me a sense of purpose and fulfillment. I felt like I was making a difference in the lives of those children, and that was incredibly rewarding.

(pauses again) You know, looking back on those times, I realize how much joy and happiness I found in simple things – spending time with loved ones, doing activities I enjoyed, feeling like I was contributing to something bigger than myself. It's funny, because now that my kids are grown and living away from home, I feel like I've lost touch with some of those feelings.

(looks down, her voice taking on a slightly wistful tone) But I'm trying to hold onto those memories, and remind myself that happiness and fulfillment can come from so many different places. It's just... it's hard when it feels like everything is revolving around my kids right now, and I'm not sure who I am outside of that.

emotions.question: Can you tell me about a specific moment or experience where you felt like yourself again, without the influence of your adult children's daily needs or concerns?
emotions.answer:
(pauses, reflecting on the question) You know, it's funny... I think one of those moments was when my husband and I decided to take a weekend trip to Lake Tahoe. We'd been feeling really cooped up at home for months, with everyone underfoot all the time, and we just needed some space to ourselves.

We packed our bags, loaded up the car, and drove up to the lake. It was one of those perfect summer days - clear blue sky, warm sunshine, and a gentle breeze. We spent the day hiking and exploring, just enjoying each other's company in peace.

At night, we sat by the campfire, watching the stars come out, and just talked about our lives. No kids, no arguments, no stress... it was like a weight had been lifted off my shoulders. I felt like myself again, you know? Like I could breathe and think clearly without all the distractions.

It was one of those moments where I realized that I'm still the same person, even if my life has changed in so many ways. And that feeling... it's hard to describe, but it's like a sense of freedom and joy that comes from knowing you're not defined by your relationships with others.

(smiles slightly) It was a small moment, maybe, but it felt like a big deal to me at the time. And looking back, I realize how much it meant to have some space to myself, to be able to recharge and remember who I am outside of being a mom or a partner.
